title: My first Steam game: 500+ outreach emails, 500k+ views, 134 sales and $0 marketing budget. Here's what I learned.
author: Cold-Rive
selftext:
# My first Steam game made $469 in 16 days with a $0 marketing budget. Here's what I learned and what I did wrong.

Hey everyone!

I released my first PC game, Tidyspell, on November 12th as a solo developer.

I wanted to share some actual numbers and talk about my marketing experience, including the things I messed up. Hopefully, this will be useful to someone preparing to release their first game.

**The numbers after 16 days:**

* Gross revenue: $469
* Net Steam revenue before Valve's cut: $391
* Steam units sold: 134
* Steam key activations: 85
* Current wishlists: 709
* Wishlists at launch: around 405
* Unique players: 101
* Median playtime: 52 minutes
* Refund rate: 5.2%
* Marketing budget: $0

My only direct expenses were the $100 Steam Direct fee and a few months of a $20 AI subscription. At least I've made that money back!

**What I did for marketing**

Most of my social media marketing was done through Twitter and Reddit.

I also sent over 500 emails to content creators, gaming channels and press outlets. This includes bulk emails, personalized emails and follow-ups, so it wasn't 500 unique contacts.

Email outreach actually worked for me. One of the biggest boosts came from a creator called Denfamonico. In total, content featuring the game received over 500,000 views.

One thing I regret is not consistently leaving my Steam page link under posts featuring my game. I could have done a better job converting some of that attention into wishlists.

**Bundles and festivals**

I started reaching out to other indie developers about making Steam bundles together.

This turned out to be more useful than I expected, and I currently have a few more bundle collaborations in the works.

Tidyspell also became part of the Tidy Up Showcase. I'd definitely recommend looking for smaller, genre-specific festivals that fit your game, especially if you don't have a marketing budget.

**My biggest mistakes**

* Missing Steam Next Fest.
* Releasing with only around 405 wishlists.
* Choosing a scope that was probably too large for my first PC game.
* Not creating enough short-form content for TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.
* Not spending enough time optimizing my Steam store page.
* Not making the most of the attention generated by content creators.

I probably could have delayed the release and spent more time building an audience. But at some point, I just wanted to finish the project and finally release a game.

**What happened after launch?**

I received a few publishing offers, particularly from Poland, and an offer to bring the game to Nintendo Switch. I decided not to move forward with them for now.

I've also released my first update, added new features, fixed bugs and expanded the game's language support to 16 languages.

There is still a lot of room for improvement, both in the game and on the Steam store page.

I'm working on new projects now, but I still want to keep Tidyspell alive through updates, bundles and short-form gameplay content.

Releasing a game doesn't mean the marketing is over. That's something I'm learning right now.

**Am I happy with the results?**

For my first game, yes.

I know these aren't impressive sales numbers, and there are many things I could have done better.

But finishing and releasing a game was more important to me than trying to make my first project a commercial success.

I now have actual experience with Steam, creator outreach, marketing, localization, publishing negotiations and post-launch support.

Hopefully, I'll make fewer mistakes with my next game. Or at least make some new ones instead of repeating the old ones :D

I'd love to hear what other developers learned from releasing their first games.
